Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block $J_n(\lambda),$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/738039128c2eef5b848f6114c6008188456705206879411c9dab82e919bc18b5.png)

In this case, we have $f(x) = 2^{x},$ $n=4,$ and $\lambda=1.$

Since $n=4,$ we need to compute the first $4-1=3$ derivatives of $f{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={2}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={2}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & ={2}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{4}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) & \frac{1}{3!}{f}^{‴}(1) \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{2}^{1} & {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} & \frac{1}{6}\cdot {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3} \\ 0 & {2}^{1} & {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \frac{1}{2}\cdot {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{1} & {2}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & {2}^{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & (\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} & \frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{3} \\ 0 & 2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & (\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block $J_n(\lambda),$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/11519fece8adb61a999a33d66d9d61e3052709066702f96b8141a4574a8d86b8.png)

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2({J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))} & ={e}^{2([\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(1) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(3)\end{aligned}])} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2({J}_{2}(1))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{2({J}_{2}(3))}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{2({J}_{2}(1))}\,⊕\,{e}^{2({J}_{2}(3))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For $J_2(1),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=1.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2\cdot 1} & 2{e}^{2\cdot 1} \\ 0 & {e}^{2\cdot 1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & 2{e}^{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For $J_2(3),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=3.$ Since $n=2,$ we need the first derivative of $f$ only, which we have already computed. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2\cdot 3} & 2{e}^{2\cdot 3} \\ 0 & {e}^{2\cdot 3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6} & 2{e}^{6} \\ 0 & {e}^{6}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

source.question: e-16517
source.value:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x) = \sin(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $V,$ we have

$$
\sin(\pi V) = \sin\left(\pi{PJP^{-1}}\right) = P \cdot (\sin(\pi J)) \cdot P^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $-3$s on the main diagonal, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/a8ad3d4a15a5a8e7307fdd6449d8086d6c9c7e656caea877d41f021c7d8584cc.png)

The derivative of $f$ is $f'(x) = \pi \cos \pi x.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/9af57a3b00b9c9e64508c119ae77690904bdb8c30b124b8165d4280149361bad.png)

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/ff9333784a9cdd38f510398b48e485764eac400f56c2cc9f2f1a18e5138845d8.png)

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi V) & =P\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi J))\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -\pi  \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\pi  & -\pi  \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\pi  & -\pi  \\ \pi  & -\pi \end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
